title: Austin Powers: The Spy Who Shagged Me
full_review:
Continuing his puerile on-screen antics, Mike Myers plays a trio of parts, including the title role, in the more-of-the-same sequel, ``Austin Powers: The Spy Who Shagged Me'' (New Line).

Once again, cocky British secret agent Powers is up against his wacky nemesis, the megalomaniacal Dr. Evil (Myers). And, after Powers' honeymoon goes bust (don't ask; it involves bride Elizabeth Hurley's surefire bust), his new sidekick is the bodacious CIA operative Felicity Shagwell (Heather Graham). The negligible story line is the flip side of the original in which cryogenically frozen Powers and Evil defrosted from the '60s into 1997; now they time-travel back to the Swinging Sixties so the spy can recover his stolen mojo (again, don't ask -- think liquid libido).

Of less importance to Austin is that the world, or at least Washington, must also be saved from Dr. Evil and his creepy cronies. Which brings us to two new villains: Mini-Me (Verne J. Troyer), a knee-high, condensed clone of the evil doctor, and a grotesquely obese Scot (Myers once more) whose character name is too crude to print and whose bodily functions are detailed with repelling regularity.

 

There are sprinklings of goofy comedy and moan-out- loud puns to be endured or enjoyed, but these alternate with gross humor and leering sexual innuendo usually appreciated by underage boys at best. The visual high point in director Jay Roach's unoriginal sequel is a vibrant musical production number with Burt Bacharach playing ``I'll Never Fall in Love Again'' on piano while Elvis Costello serenades Austin and Felicity amid a riot of color and wild prints on the mod and miniskirted passers-by.

On the downside, those viewers previously spared the sight of TV talk-show host Jerry Springer orchestrating chaos among his guests will be subject to just that when Dr. Evil appears in a scene as Springer's verbally and physically combative guest to express his ire that his only son, Scott Evil (Seth Green), isn't living up to his name. A meant-to-be-clever opening-credit scene has Austin gallivanting in the buff through a crowded hotel with precisely positioned credits, foliage, bananas or sausages barely saving the movie from a more restrictive rating.

Visually stretched to the limit, the lame sight gag soon goes limp, although another racy section also dealing with male private parts features some amusing sound editing from scene to scene.

 All in all, the silly sequel breaks no new ground, confident of its continuing appeal after theatrical success and astounding video sales. If anything, it's a triumph of tastelessness in a pop culture enamored of all things dumb and dumber.

The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned that some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
